# The two versions of largest, transliterated into Python so we can count calls.
# car(L) is L[0]; cdr(L) is L[1:]; (null? (cdr L)) is len(L) == 1.

calls = {"largest": 0, "largest2": 0}

def largest(L):
    calls["largest"] += 1
    if len(L) == 1:
        return L[0]
    if L[0] >= largest(L[1:]):      # first recursive call
        return L[0]
    return largest(L[1:])           # second recursive call, same work again

def largest2(L):
    calls["largest2"] += 1
    if len(L) == 1:
        return L[0]
    largestval = largest2(L[1:])    # computed ONCE, then named
    return L[0] if L[0] >= largestval else largestval

for n in (4, 8, 12, 16):
    data = list(range(1, n + 1))    # worst case: the largest element is last
    calls["largest"] = calls["largest2"] = 0
    assert largest(data) == largest2(data) == n
    print(f"  n = {n:2d}   largest: {calls['largest']:6d} calls    "
          f"largest2: {calls['largest2']:3d} calls")

print()
print("  Same answer, same shape, wildly different cost: doubling every level")
print("  against one call per level.  The only difference in the source is that")
print("  largest2 names the subresult with let instead of recomputing it.")
description: Measure how naming a recursive subresult once in largest2 keeps call counts linear, while recomputing it in largest doubles the work at each level.

steps.description: Lines 4-12 transliterate Scheme's `largest` into Python and increment `calls["largest"]` on every call. When `L[0] >= largest(L[1:])` on line 10 is `False`, line 12 calls `largest(L[1:])` a second time on the exact same slice.

`largest2(L)` increments `calls["largest2"]` on line 15. It calls `largest2(L[1:])` once on line 18 and stores the result in `largestval`. Line 19 can both compare and return it without a second recursive call.
Compare lines 10-12 with lines 18-19: `largest` branches into a second recursive call whenever `L[0]` is smaller than the maximum of `L[1:]`, whereas `largest2` reuses `largestval`.
Lines 21-27 test `n` in `(4, 8, 12, 16)` on ascending lists `list(range(1, n + 1))`. The largest element is at the end, so `L[0] >= ...` is `False` at every level.

steps.answer: `largest(data)` makes `15` calls ($2^4 - 1$, doubling at each level), while `largest2(data)` makes `4` calls (one per element).
steps.question: For `n = 4` (`data = [1, 2, 3, 4]`), how many calls does `largest(data)` make compared to `largest2(data)`?

steps.description: At trace step 20 inside `largest([3, 4])`, `3 >= largest([4])` has just evaluated to `False`, so line 12 calls `largest([4])` a second time.

title: Counting Recursive Calls: largest vs. largest2
